name: Feature browser screenshot
summary: A screengrab of the paper's published feature browser with arrows and captions added for print: one page lays four separate kinds of evidence about a single learned feature side by side, and the search strip shows what could be asked of a whole run. It is not one chart with one axis, and everything outside the grey panel is annotation the tool itself never prints.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The paper's case for any one [[feature]] is a fixed list of claims — the [[feature-evidence-template|five-claim template]] — each in a different unit: a purity fraction, a next-token [[logit-weight]], a correlation against neurons, a firing rate. No shared axis, so no single plot. The screenshot puts all four on one screen so a reader can check they agree about the same feature. A table of the same numbers would hide what the paper needs visible: whether the interpretation survives below the top of the activation range, where interpretations usually fail.

The second reason is self-selection. Run A/1 has 4,096 features and Section 3 discusses four ([[cherry-picked-case-studies|four the authors chose]]). An average would let them pick what to average, and judging a unit by its strongest firings flatters it ([[max-dataset-example-bias]]). Publishing the [[feature-exploration-interface|browser]] hands the check over: a reader can open a feature the paper never mentions. The search strip is the other half of that offer — no results, only the shape of question the authors could put to a whole [[dictionary-learning-run|run]].

### How to read it, step by step

Everything outside the grey panel is annotation added for the paper. The tool prints none of it.

The header is identity: an index within the run ([[feature-notation|#3923]]), a hand-written label — `Latin: ?`, the question mark flagging an unsure labeller ([[manual-interpretability-scoring]]) — and a machine-written explanation scored $0.305$ ([[automated-interpretability]], [[activation-prediction-scoring]]).

Then four columns. First, three comparison tables. NEURON ALIGNMENT writes the [[feature-direction]] out in the basis of the 512 MLP neurons ([[neuron-basis-coefficients]]); CORRELATED NEURONS ranks neurons instead by how closely their activations track the feature's ([[most-correlated-neuron]], by [[pearson-correlation]]); CORRELATED B FEATURES runs that comparison against a dictionary trained on [[transformer-a-and-b|a second transformer differing only in seed]], which is [[universality]] measured as [[activation-similarity]].

Second column holds the only real axes. The upper histogram has [[feature-activation]] on $x$ — a ReLU output, so non-negative — and counts of randomly sampled tokens on $y$. Exact zeros are dropped, so it shows how the feature fires, not how often; how often is the header's $	ext{DENSITY} = 0.1440\%$ ([[feature-density]]). Below it, logit weights over the vocabulary, centred because softmax is shift-invariant, ten tokens of each tail listed above.

Third column, the [[top-dataset-examples|top 20 activating examples]]; fourth, ten evenly spaced [[activation-interval|subsample intervals]] stepping down from the maximum — $11.54$, then $10.04$, $9.168$ — each printing its own ceiling.

A token carries two encodings at once. Orange background is activation strength; the underline is a separate experiment, a [[feature-ablation]], blue where the feature had been helping that token's prediction and red where it had been hurting ([[ablation-effect-visualization]]). Bold marks the selected token, with four tokens of context each side.

Look at CORRELATED NEURONS first, then the low intervals; the top examples are the least informative panel here.

The search strip reads left to right as one query: a matching mode, the field matched against, a sort key over every feature in the run, and Underline Mode, which decides whether underlines mean one feature ablated or the whole MLP activation swapped for the autoencoder's reconstruction ([[loss-recovered-by-features]]).

### What a bad result would look like

Here the best correlated neuron reaches $+0.09$ and the best matching B-run feature $+0.75$. Flip either and the page collapses. A neuron near $0.9$ would mean [[dictionary-learning]] had handed back a neuron under a new name; a best B feature near $0.1$ would mean an artifact of one seed. Coherent top examples above interval bands that read as noise would mean the interpretation holds only at the very top. A logit histogram with no tails would mean the feature does nothing downstream.

The page does not hide its weak spots, which is part of what it is for: the label is a shrug and $0.305$ is above chance but far from a match. The search figure cannot come out badly at all — it shows a control panel, not a result.

### Where it comes back

As a whole shape, only here: fig-4 and fig-5. Its panels return separately through Section 3 — activation histograms, logit tails, neuron comparisons, shaded and underlined text — so the anatomy is worth learning once. A second tool, listing every feature active on one dataset example, is screenshotted the same way in fig-6 ([[data-oriented-interface]]). The same page in a wider dictionary is where [[feature-splitting]] shows: one feature's territory split across several pages that each look like this.
